**Three stop-and-reports, none silently resolved.** Platform-admin cross-tenant reads are NOT

(`user_memberships`, `§4`'s second named path, already on the list; the other two cross a

**⚠ AND TWO OF THOSE FOUR CLOSURES WERE CLAIMED BEFORE THEY WERE WRITTEN.** This section and the

#### ⚠ THE ONE GATE CLAUSE THIS TASK DOES NOT MEET

`§3` row 5 requires *"passkey registration + login proven end to end **through the browser**
against the harness page"*. **It is not met, and it cannot be from this machine.** The credential
ceremony lives in `navigator.credentials`, not in HTTP, so a valid attestation needs a real
authenticator or a virtual one over CDP. Measured 2026-10-28: `which chromium chromium-browser
google-chrome firefox node` returns nothing but a Windows `npx` shim, and `~/.cache/ms-playwright`
does not exist. The harness page IS built and mounted outside `production`, and every
server-side half IS tested — options issued and the challenge kept server-side, each options
call replacing the pending challenge, a credential with no stored challenge refused, a malformed
one refused, the user handle an HMAC rather than the user id. **What was NOT done is fabricate an
attestation and call it end-to-end**, which is the vacuous-assertion defect this section records
four of, committed on purpose. Carried as **`R-100`**, owned by Task 9 — whose gate already
requires Playwright, so the browser exists there by construction.

#### Nine defects the suite found that the builder had wrong

Listed because each is one a reviewer would otherwise have to find, and because every one was
found by a test rather than by reading:

1. **deptrac refused `App\Features\Devices` → `App\Platform\Auth`** — the rule Task 5 had
   just repurposed, biting its own author. The tenant-pin **encoding** moved to
   `App\Domain\Auth\TenantPin`, which both sides read.
2. **`R-052`'s control caught internal rationale in PUBLISHED descriptions, twice** — first a
   form-request rule comment, then a class docblock. Scramble ships both as the OpenAPI
   `description`. The rationale now lives in plain `/* */` blocks, which are not docblocks.
   **`R-052`'s compensating control, which `R-052` itself records as never having worked, worked
   here.**
3. **Sanctum's token model assumes a bigint key** — `23502` null violation on `id`, measured
   through the real endpoint. Second instance of the mismatch the passkey model already had, so
   it is recorded as a pattern rather than fixed twice in silence.
4. **The `api` group had NO session middleware**, so `$request->hasSession()` was false and the
   tenant selection silently never applied — and **every single-membership test still passed**,
   because the resolver falls back to `Memberships::sole()`. Only a user with TWO memberships
   exposed it. A fallback that hides a broken primary path is worse than no fallback.
5. **`User::refresh()` bypasses global scopes**, so it emitted `select *` and hit the `42501`
   the scope exists to prevent. Fixed in the **model**, not just the caller — a caller fix would
   have left the next `refresh()` anywhere to find it again. Residual class carried as `R-103`.
6. **`encrypted` casts on the two 2FA columns double-encrypted them** — Fortify owns that
   encryption end to end. `DecryptException: The payload is invalid.`
7. **Withholding the 2FA secrets from the app role broke Fortify's own helpers**, which read
   them off the model. That is what `public.user_two_factor(uuid)` is for, in its own migration
   rather than an edit to the applied one, which is `R-003`'s closure rule.
8. **A test asserted a tri-state the code did not have** — a session selection that is *present
   but unusable* must refuse, not fall back, because falling back made a corrupted session act in
   a tenant nobody chose, and for a single-membership user that succeeds and looks normal. **The
   test was right and the code changed.**
9. **`RequireAbility`'s fail-closed claim was true of a SUBSET of the surface, not of it.** It is
   wrapped round a group in `routes/v1.php`, so it reaches routes somebody remembered to nest in
   that group — and a staff route added elsewhere in the file would have been served with no
   authorisation check at all. Measured: an ad-hoc `/v1` route on the `api` group answered **200**.
   **The obvious fix was tried and reverted**: moving the middleware onto the `api` group reaches
   every `/v1` route, and it also reaches the ad-hoc unnamed probe routes nine test files mount
   there, so twenty-odd tests went red on infrastructure rather than on behaviour — and letting an
   unnamed route through is the fail-open the middleware exists to prevent. So the property is
   stated as **two layers** instead of being claimed away: the runtime check fails closed inside
   the group, and `RoleMatrixTest`'s closed-world check over the whole router is what catches a
   route added outside it. Both the route file and the test say so.

#### Two design reversals, both recorded in `§1`

**The tenant came from an `X-Tenant` header in the first draft, and the DESIGN changed rather
than the test.** `PagerIdorTest` › *does not let a tenant id be chosen by anything the caller
sends* already drives five shapes — `X-Tenant-Id`, **`X-Tenant`**, `?tenant_id=`, and two body
fields — and requires **404** from each. A header resolver turns that into a 401: still a
refusal, but it would have meant weakening an existing invariant test to fit new code. The
selection moved into the server-side session and the pin into the token, and **that IDOR case
passes unchanged**.

**And `personal_access_tokens` carries no `tenant_id`.** A column makes it a tenant table, C4
then forces RLS, and the row becomes invisible to the lookup that must happen before any tenant
is known — whose only escape is a **fifth** named cross-tenant path that `§4` forbids without a
rank-2 edit. So the tenant travels in `abilities` as a **claim**, verified against the holder's
own memberships on every request. This is the assumption the handover flags as most worth a
reviewer's disagreement.

### Task 5 — the `§11` reviews of 2026-10-28, and the single fix pass they produced

Two reviewers, run **concurrently in separate sessions**, each given only
`git diff task-4...task-5-auth-rbac` and `docs/tickets/QRPAGER-12.md` — never each other's
output, never the handover, never this session's reasoning. Separate checklists, separate
order, never merged.

**31 findings. QA 19 (0 Critical · 1 High · 9 Medium · 9 Low) · Security 12 (1 Critical ·
2 High · 4 Medium · 5 Low).** Both counts are stated separately and the combined total
matches the list below, which is `§11`'s relay rule.

**The named invariant held.** Neither reviewer could falsify *a tenant-provisioning actor
cannot read another tenant's data*, and QA revert-proved it: replacing the membership
verification in `Memberships::in()` with a fabricated membership reddens
`PlatformAdminIsNotABypassTest` twice with assertion failures. The stub-removal clause held
too, checked by both against the zero-hit assertion rather than the claim.

**One gate clause WAS falsified, and it is the Critical.** `§4.3`'s second clause, *device
token scope cannot escalate*, failed on the one surface `RequestPrincipal` is never consulted
on — see C-1.

#### What the Critical was, because it is the whole shape of this round

`routes/auth.php` is mounted on the `auth-surface` group, which carries the session stack and
`ResolvePrincipal` and — deliberately, for reasons that still hold — neither
`RequireTenantScope` (circular: the tenant comes from the credential a login is about to
establish) nor `RequireAbility` (no tenant yet to hold an ability in). `ResolvePrincipal` tries
the `web` guard then `sanctum`, so a KDS device is authenticated rather than 401'd on the one
route its ability permits. Both decisions are right.

Together they left every auth route's only gate as the controller's own
`$request->user() instanceof User` — **and a bearer token satisfies that test.** Driven by the
reviewer against the composed Postgres with a token minted exactly as `DeviceTokens::issue`
does (abilities `['tenant:<A>', 'pager:read']`, one tenant, one read-only capability), held by
a user who owns tenants A **and** B:

| request with the KDS bearer | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/pager-sessions` | 200 — its one legitimate ability | **200**, unchanged |
| `GET /v1/members`, `POST /v1/devices` | 403 — the staff surface held | 403 |
| `GET /v1/auth/me` | **200** — name, email, `is_platform_admin`, and **every membership including tenant B's id, slug and role** | **403** |
| `POST /v1/auth/two-factor/enable` | **200** — a fresh TOTP secret and all **8** recovery codes | **403** |
| `DELETE /v1/auth/two-factor` | **204** — second factor removed | **403** |
| `GET /v1/auth/passkeys/options` | **200** — challenge plus the victim's WebAuthn handle and display name | **403** |
| `POST /v1/auth/tenant` | **204** | **403** |

Anonymous requests to those routes answered **401** throughout, which isolates the bearer
token as the thing that authorised them. Re-keying was measured separately: enrol → confirm
with a real OTP → the device token calls `enable` again → **a different secret is returned and
`two_factor_confirmed_at` is unchanged.** The legitimate authenticator stops working and the
secret in force is the attacker's. Chained — `passkeys/options` → `POST /v1/auth/passkeys` →
`POST /v1/auth/passkeys/login`, all on the same gate — that is a full staff session as an
owner of every tenant the issuer belongs to. The one step the reviewer could not execute is
the WebAuthn ceremony itself, which is `R-100`; **every HTTP gate in front of it was measured
open.**

`RoleMatrixTest` could not see it: its `$auth` set is a bare **name allowlist**, and
membership in it asserts nothing about who may call a route. Its comment even read
"`challenge` is the only one reachable without a session" — every one of the twelve was
reachable with a `pager:read` bearer token.

**The fix is `App\Platform\Http\Middleware\RefuseDeviceToken`, on the group and not per
controller**, so a route added to `routes/auth.php` inherits the refusal instead of having to
remember it. It refuses on credential SHAPE (`DeviceToken::isTokenRequest`), leaves anonymous
requests untouched so login and the two ceremonies stay reachable, and leaves a staff session
carrying a stray `Authorization` header untouched because `ResolvePrincipal` tries `web`
first. `DeviceTokenOnAuthSurfaceTest` drives **all thirteen routes on the group** — the twelve
plus `/passkey-harness` — enumerates the group from the live router so coverage cannot drift,
and was proven red first: `GET /v1/auth/me` → 200.

#### Disposition

Under the standing rulings: Critical/High fixed with a regression test proven red without the
fix; a false claim corrected in place and never a `§5` row; Medium/Low fixed where small and
local, else a `§5` row with owner and date; one root reached by both reviewers = one fix, two
labelled entries.

**Of 31: 23 fixed in code or tests · 5 false claims corrected in place · 2 deferred outright ·
1 already a `§5` row (`R-101`). 28 of the 31 therefore had a change land**, and **four new rows,
`R-104`…`R-107`** — two of which sit BESIDE a fix, because two findings split into a defect half
that was fixed and a policy half that was not this task's to decide. Every one of them is in
**one pass and one push**, not finding by finding.

⚠ **The fix commit's own message says "26 fixed", and that figure is wrong.** It was written
before the table below was classified row by row, and it conflated the 23 code fixes with the
5 in-place corrections while dropping two. The correct split is the one above; it is recorded
here rather than amended away, because re-writing the commit would invalidate the
three-green-runs transcript that names its SHA — and because this ledger's own standard is

#### A defect this pass committed and caught, recorded because `§4a` is where they go

The first version of SEC M-4's test was **vacuous**, and it is the fifth of this class on this
branch. `expect($log)->not->toContain($value, $message)` — Pest's `toContain` takes
**variadic needles**, not a needle and a message, so negated it asserted "the log contains
neither the value nor that sentence", which the absent sentence satisfied on its own. It
passed against the unfixed redactor. Caught by running it against the unfixed code rather
than by reading it, which is the only thing that ever catches this.

The project already had the control: `SourceGuard::VACUOUS_NEGATED_CONTAINS`, with its own
fixtures and a `RepoGuardTest` case scoping the exception to one function. **It would have
caught this instance on the next full-suite run** — the guard worked; the author got there
first. Four other files already carry `str_contains()` with a comment saying exactly why.

The same discipline found one more: `bin/migration-rollback-proof`'s new **absence** checks
would have passed against an empty fingerprint, so the script now proves the file non-empty
for the tables those checks concern before making them, and prints the 67 grant lines as
evidence.

#### One thing deliberately not changed, stated rather than dropped

**`/passkey-harness` is still unmetered**, and SEC H-2 named it alongside `me` and `logout`.
The other two are fixed; this one is left, and the reason is the reviewer's own bounding of
it: the route is **absent from the route table under `APP_ENV=production`** — they verified
that out of process, and `RouteSurfaceTest` plus `bootstrap/app.php`'s condition are what
keep it so. It renders a static Blade view, opens no database connection and now refuses a
device bearer token like every other route on the group. A bucket on it would also be the one
limiter in the project that could make **Task 9's browser E2E run** fail in a way that looks
like a passkey defect rather than a rate limit, which is a poor trade for a dev-only page.

So: no bucket, and `routes/auth.php`'s "EVERY ROUTE HERE NAMES A BUCKET" is scoped to that
file, which is where it is written. If that reasoning is wrong the fix is one line — it is
recorded here rather than left for a reader to notice the exception.

#### Two test-harness divergences met while fixing, both `R-102`

Neither is a production defect and both are recorded rather than papered over. `Memberships`
memoises per user for the life of a request and the suite's container outlives the request, so
a suspension applied after an HTTP call is invisible to the next one — measured, 2 memberships
instead of 1, and **neither `forgetScopedInstances()` nor `forgetInstance()` cleared it on that
path**, so the case was restructured to make no request before suspending, which is why
`RoleMatrixTest`'s suspended case does not need the flush either. Separately, the `sanctum`
guard stays resolved between requests, so a loop that used a bearer token in one iteration had
its next iteration's **login** refused 403 by `RefuseDeviceToken` — the new middleware reading
a guard that production rebuilds per request.

### Task 5 — the `§11` review of the FIX DIFF, round 1, and the second pass it produced (2026-10-28)

`§11`'s round limit allows the fix diff two reviews. This is the first; both reviewers ran
concurrently in separate sessions, each given only `git diff 59b22b0..6e5847d` and the
ticket — **not** `§4a`'s record above, which is this session's reasoning.

**24 findings. QA 12 (0 Critical · 1 High · 5 Medium · 6 Low) · Security 12 (0 Critical ·
1 High · 4 Medium · 7 Low).** Counts stated separately; the combined total matches the list.

**Neither named gate clause is falsified, and both reviewers confirmed the round-1 Critical
closed** — independently, and more thoroughly than the fix was tested: a real `pager:read`
token minted through `POST /v1/devices` was refused on all thirteen routes, with a positive
control first (200 on its own board), with header-shape variants (`authorization` lowercase,
`BEARER` uppercase, `?token=`, `X-Auth-Token`) all refused, and with valid CSRF pairs on the
nine state-changing routes. A low-privilege session presenting another user's device token
got its OWN identity back, so `ResolvePrincipal`'s web-first order is not a confusion
channel. The `FOR UPDATE` fix was falsified-then-confirmed: one reviewer instrumented both
children and showed the critical sections genuinely overlap (entered 0.1 ms apart, ~23 ms
each), then reproduced 0 owners against the pre-fix rule.

#### Both Highs were in the fixes this session had just written

**Security's High — the limiter ran behind the group it was meant to bound.** Laravel runs
group middleware before route middleware. The five auth buckets are named per route, and the
`auth-surface` group carries the session stack, `ValidateCsrfToken`, `ResolvePrincipal` and
`RefuseDeviceToken` — so every refusal those four produce happened before any bucket was
consulted. Measured at 100 requests per form:

| form | result | cost per request, unmetered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/auth/me`, valid device token | 100 × 403, **zero 429** | Redis session r/w + one `personal_access_tokens` SELECT + 322 bytes of ERROR log |
| `GET /v1/auth/me`, `Bearer zzz\|q` — **no credential needed** | 100 × 422, **zero 429** | one FAILED Postgres statement + 345 bytes of ERROR log |
| `POST /v1/auth/login`, no CSRF token — **no credential needed** | 100 × 419, **zero 429** | one new Redis session key, 120-minute TTL (measured 332 → 392 keys over 60 requests) |
| the same malformed bearer against `GET /v1/pager-sessions` | 120 × 422 then **20 × 429** | metered — the `api` group has the ordering right |

The last row is the attack: an unauthenticated caller fills the session store, and **Redis is
also the limiter's own backend** — `RateLimit` fails OPEN when it cannot reach Redis
(`R-027`), so filling it removes every bucket in the project. And the route comment this
session wrote claiming `me`'s lookup "is BOUNDED" was false for exactly the same reason:
`ResolvePrincipal` performs that lookup before the limiter runs.

Fixed by a coarse `auth-surface` bucket **first in the group**, which is the ordering
`bootstrap/app.php` already argues for on the `api` group twenty lines down. Three forms
driven to a real 429, each proven red first at 422, 419 and 403 respectively, each with a
positive control asserting the first two requests are refused by the middleware under test
and not by the limiter. A fourth case pins that the per-route buckets are still the policy —
a login must not silently get 120/min because the group now counts.

**QA's High — the regression test for the passkey name bound could not fail.** It asserted
only `assertStatus(422)`, and the vendor's `passedValidation()` answers 422 for any credential
a test can fabricate whatever the name is; deleting the guard left the file green at 9 passed.
The cause was the FIX, not the test: an `mb_strlen()` check in the controller is unreachable,
because the vendor deserialises in `passedValidation()` which runs only once validation has
passed. So `§6`'s "a regression test that fails without the fix" was literally unmet, and the
guard could have been deleted with a green suite.

The bound is now a **validation rule** in this project's own `PasskeyRegistrationRequest`,
which runs *before* deserialisation — and that makes the two refusals tell apart, so the test
asserts WHICH one happened: `errors.name` for 121 characters, `errors.credential` for 120.
Proven red by restoring `max:255`.

#### The correction that matters most, because it is about a Critical's impact

QA finding 5. `ValidateCsrfToken` runs **before** `RefuseDeviceToken` in the group, so a
bearer-ONLY client — no session cookie, no CSRF token — was **already refused 419** on every
state-changing route. The round-1 figures for `two-factor/enable` (200, a fresh secret and
eight recovery codes), `two-factor/disable` (204), the registration ceremony and
`auth/tenant` (204) were taken through the TEST harness, where
`ValidateCsrfToken::runningUnitTests()` turns CSRF off. They are true as test-harness
measurements and they are **not** the production blast radius.

**What a bearer token alone genuinely reached is the two GETs:** `auth.me`'s whole
cross-tenant membership map, and `passkeys/options`' live challenge plus the victim's WebAuthn
handle and display name. Both are cross-tenant disclosures from a credential whose entire
scope is one tenant and one read-only capability — which is the named invariant failing, so
**the fix stands on the GETs alone without the larger claim.**

**And the POSTs were reachable in one shape that is not hypothetical:** a stolen kitchen
screen that still holds a live session cookie *and* its matching CSRF token, which is exactly
what a browser-based KDS on a shared screen has. In that shape the full list applies.

Corrected in `RefuseDeviceToken`, `DeviceTokenOnAuthSurfaceTest`, `TwoFactorController` and
the round-1 table above. The same correction retires this session's claim that the refusal is
"the same answer everywhere": in production nine of the thirteen are CSRF's 419, not
`RefuseDeviceToken`'s 403. Still refused, refused sooner, and not one answer.

#### Three defects this session introduced while fixing, and how each was caught

Worth naming together, because they are one pattern: **a fix written confidently and not run
against the thing it was supposed to break.**

1. **A test that could not fail** (QA's High) — caught by the reviewer deleting the guard.
2. **An absence check that could never fire** — caught by the reviewer re-granting the
   privilege and diffing the fingerprint.
3. **A docblock published into `docs/openapi.json`** — `R-052`'s defect for the third time on
   this branch, caught by `composer openapi:check` in this session's own gate run. The project
   already had the convention (`LoginRequest`: *"INTERNAL NOTES -- not a docblock, because a
   docblock here is published as the request body's schema description"*) and the new class
   did not follow it. The same class also made Scramble publish a
   `403 AuthorizationException` with an `application/json` body — two non-problem-document
   responses on a surface where every refusal is one — which declaring `authorize()`
   explicitly removed.

And a fourth, caught in the same pass: the first version of this round's `TransientToken`
assertion passed `request()`, the test's ambient request with no user resolver, so it returned
false with the broken predicate too. Vacuous, in the file written to fix vacuous assertions.
Every one of the four was found by running the new test against the unfixed code, which is the
only thing that ever finds them.

0 High · 4 Medium · 5 Low).**

**Neither named gate clause is falsified, by either reviewer, explicitly stated by both.**
Security re-drove the round-1 Critical closed independently and with a genuinely minted token

it was asked to falsify and every one survived.

#### The two that had to be acted on

**Both reviewers found that `docs/PLAN.md` was not in the commit.** `R-108`…`R-111` and the
whole round-1 disposition table existed only as a 149-line uncommitted working-tree change,
while **committed code cited `R-108` four times** — including two test FAILURE MESSAGES
telling the next engineer to go read it. `git show c3c4337:docs/PLAN.md | grep -c R-108` → 0.
That is the same defect this branch corrected three times one level up (`MatrixCoverageTest`,
`MembershipScopeTest`, `AuthContractTest` — all named, none existing), arrived at by splitting
a commit. Fixed by committing the record **with** the code that cites it, and the rule worth
keeping is narrower than "never split": do not split when committed code names the row.

**Security found a THIRD `SECURITY DEFINER` seam, and it is the worst of them.**
`public.authenticate_user(varchar)` returns `password_hash`, so one lateral join yields a real
bcrypt hash for every account with a password — measured at 14 of 20 rows. `R-006`'s entire
closure is that `qrpager_app` cannot read `users.password`, and `2026_10_28_140000` dropped
`two_factor_secret` from this very function for exactly that reason while leaving the hash in
it. `R-108` named "the two readers" and `MembershipEnumerationTest` pinned two and stopped, so
**the strongest instance was outside the scope of the row that was about to be accepted.**
`R-108` is widened to three, a third case drives it, and its review-by says to take the
password hash first — a membership map is metadata and the 2FA secret is ciphertext needing
`APP_KEY`; a bcrypt hash is an offline-crackable credential on its own.

#### What this round says about the previous one

Eight of the seventeen were defects introduced while fixing: a vacuous assertion, a
nondeterministic assertion count, a lost operational datum, a false claim left standing in the
file being changed, a count corrected wrongly, a justification stated from an uncommitted
state, a scan over constants, and a positive control coupled to an open risk. Plus the
uncommitted record.

That is the same pattern `§4a` already records twice on this branch, and the round-2 record
above named it: **a fix written confidently and not run against the thing it was supposed to
break.** The four reviewer runs over this task found 55 findings; of those, **eleven were in
code this session had written in response to an earlier finding.** The ratio is the useful
number, and it is the argument for the round limit existing rather than against it — each
round found less, and round 2 found no Critical and no invariant failure.

**What the reviews could not do, and said so:** `R-100` is untouched by any of it. Passkey
registration and login are still not proven through a browser, both reviewers confirmed the
clause is NOT MET, and it remains the one gate clause on this task with no evidence behind it.

### Task 6 — **built, reviewed to `§11`, fixed in ONE pass, and tagged `task-6`** on `task-6-provisioning` (2026-10-28). Ticket `QRPAGER-13`, epic E4

Branch cut from the `task-5` tag (`5a227f8`). **No PR and no merge, by instruction** — `main`
stays untouched until client handover (`§10`), so the tag is the delivery record.

#### What this task is, in one paragraph

The ruling of 2026-10-28 (rank 1, and `QRPAGER-13 §0`) settled `§3.1` row 6's standing
blocker **by a different design rather than by a fifth named cross-tenant path**: platform
tables are not tenant tables, the panel operates only on tables belonging to no tenant, and
per-tenant statistics are aggregates written to a platform table by a job inside the tenant.
So `§4 › Tenancy`'s named list is **unchanged**, `RlsCoverageTest`'s "exactly the four named
cross-tenant policies" is untouched, and **no grant on any tenant table was widened**.

Three new PLATFORM tables, none under RLS: `tenant_provisionings` (the provisioning record
and the registry the panel lists, written *before* the tenant exists), `tenant_statistics`
(aggregates, one row per tenant), `platform_audit_log` (append-only by `ENABLE ALWAYS`
triggers). Filament **v5.11.0** on Laravel **13.38.0**, both verified by running code.

#### The figures, each at the commit it was measured at

| | |

#### The `§11` reviews — 32 findings, and the two that were real defects in this code

Both ran **concurrently in two separate sessions**, each given only
`git diff task-5...task-6-provisioning` and `docs/tickets/QRPAGER-13.md`: never each other's
output, never the handover, never this session's reasoning.

**QA 19 — 0 Critical, 2 High, 8 Medium, 9 Low. Security 13 — 0 Critical, 2 High, 3 Medium,
8 Low. Combined 32 — 0 Critical, 4 High, 11 Medium, 17 Low.** All 32 dispositioned in one
pass. **The named invariant held in both reviews, both reviewers said so explicitly, and
neither found a Critical.**

**SECURITY H-1 IS THE ONE THAT MATTERED, and it is the shape this project keeps paying for.**
The aggregate job read `pager_sessions` on the **worker** connection inside each tenant's
scope, and its own docblock called that "an ordinary scoped read". `qrpager_worker` carries
`worker_reads_expired_sessions`, a **permissive** cross-tenant SELECT policy
`USING (expires_at <= now() AND status IN ('waiting','ready','expired'))` — and permissive
policies are **OR-ed**. So inside tenant A's scope the job also saw every other tenant's
past-TTL sessions, which in the production steady state is most of them: every tenant's
counters, percentiles and window bounds were contaminated, and one reviewer measured a
`window_start` that predated the tenant's own existence. Measured independently in the fix
session: **worker 4 rows over 2 tenants where the app role sees 1 over 1.**

`§2.6` already records this exact asymmetry — *"⚠ AND IT BOUNDS THE CONTEXT-FREE PATH ONLY"*,
from Task 3's security L-2 — and it was read during this task's own Phase 0 and **not
connected to the design being written**. That is the finding worth keeping: the trap was
documented, in this file, and the documentation did not fire.

Fixed with **two independent bounds**, only one of which lives in the file: the reads moved
to the **app** connection, which holds no cross-tenant policy on any table
(`RlsCoverageTest` pins that), **and** each aggregate statement carries
`where tenant_id = ?` explicitly. Revert-proved: the faithful revert fails with
`4 is identical to 1`.

**SECURITY H-2** — no rate limiter on any of the four panel routes or on Livewire's update
endpoint, while every `/v1` route, the auth group and even the 404 fallback carried one. The
cost was measured rather than argued: each anonymous 401 or 419 minted **one Redis session
key with a 7 200 s TTL**, because `StartSession` persists a session to carry a CSRF token
*before* `Authenticate` refuses — on a path needing no credential, in the store `§1` locks
for session **and** cache **and** queue. A `panel` bucket now runs first in the panel's
middleware list and reaches Livewire's endpoint through the `web` group, whose only members
are Livewire's three routes (asserted, so a future member is a deliberate act).

**THE OTHER TWO HIGHS WERE RECORD DEFECTS, AND BOTH WERE THIS SESSION'S.** QA H-1 / security
M-3: `R-114`…`R-118` were cited in the ticket, in a test's header and in a code comment while
appearing **zero** times in this file, and `R-106` still named Task 6 although the ticket
claimed it had been re-owned — the "claimed before written" pattern `§0`'s debt cell records
for `R-003`, `R-004`, `R-006` and `R-035` before it. QA H-2 / security L-2: `attempts` was
incremented, selected and read by **nothing**, while three documents claimed "retries bounded
by `attempts`" and a docblock named a `--retry-stalled` option that did not exist — `R-058`'s
shape (a column selected and never read) reproduced in new code, with the consequence that a
row left at `running` was stuck for ever and recoverable only by the hand SQL `§3` row 6
forbids.

#### Four things this task's own instruments got wrong, and one figure it published wrongly

1. **`bin/provisioning-revert-proof` took its restore copy from the WORKING TREE** (`cp` to a
   temp file) rather than from git. With a concurrent reviewer session in the same checkout
   that restored the *other* session's revert and reported it byte-identical — truthfully, to
   the wrong baseline — and one reviewer's run consequently measured the invariant case
   **green**, the opposite of what was published. It now refuses a dirty tree and restores
   with `git checkout --`.
2. **⚠ "REVERT A TURNS 8 CASES RED" WAS PUBLISHED AND IS WRONG.** Six of those reds were
   `ErrorException`s from a revert that split the transaction with a pattern and left
   `$ownerUserId` undefined — the harness breaking, not the guard being removed, which is the
   precise thing `bin/_revert-proof.sh` exists to reject. **Two** genuine assertion reds carry
   the transactional clause. `ErrorException`, `TypeError`, `Undefined variable` and their
   family are in the not-evidence list now, and revert A is written out by hand in
   `bin/support/revert-split-transaction.py` rather than assembled by a regex.
3. **The listener half of the named invariant's proof had never been seen red** (QA M-1). The
   runtime scope guard refuses an *unscoped* statement before it is sent, so `DB::listen`
   never fired and the red arrived from a status assertion sharing the same case. The status
   check is now its own case, and **revert C** reads a tenant table *inside* a scope — the
   case the guard allows and only the listener catches.
4. **`revert_proof_run` never required a revert to produce any red at all** (QA L-4), so an
   edit that silently matched nothing would have passed while the verdict printed "every
   revert kept its controls green and every red was an assertion" — true, and vacuous. Each
   revert now declares a **required red**, and the fragment must be short because Pest
   truncates case names, which was itself measured here by a false alarm.

Also: **three of this session's own assertions were the vacuous
`not->toContain($needle, $message)` shape**, caught by `SourceGuard` rule 7 — the control
working on the very assertions carrying this task's named invariant. And `composer gate`, the
form `CLAUDE.md` mandates *because* it leaves readable evidence, was running inside composer's
300 s `process-timeout` against a ~270 s suite; both reviewers hit the truncation. Fixed with
`Composer\Config::disableProcessTimeout`, which this repository already does for `dev`.

#### What this task does NOT deliver — named, with owners

`§3` row 6's four clauses are quoted and answered one at a time in `§3.1` row 6. Two are not
met and one is met by substitution:

- **"a scannable QR in one wizard pass"** — needs `pager_sessions`. **`R-115`, Task 10.**
- **"platform admin actions all land in `audit_log`"** — **measured impossible** for a serving
  process (42501 on insert in and out of context, 0 rows on read; owner-with-bypass only). Met
  against `platform_audit_log`. A **false claim corrected in place**, not a `§5` row.
- **"a staff invite is actually delivered"** — **`R-124`, Task 10**, and separately from
  `R-115` on purpose: the ruling is no obstacle to it at all, since delivering mail touches no
  tenant table. The honest reason is that no invite is minted here. Conflating the two was
  itself QA M-7.
- Staff-management screens and QR batch generation — **`R-115`**. ⚠ And the *reason* is
  narrower than first written: these are not unreachable by this task's architecture, which
  writes two tenant tables out of band from a scheduled command inside the tenant's own
  context. What the ruling forbids is doing it **on the panel's request**.

**Eleven new `§5` rows, `R-114` … `R-124`, none Critical or High, all swept into `§3.2`'s
seventeenth delta the same day. `R-106` is RE-OWNED to Task 10, not closed** — on the
rank-2-edit reason alone, the second reason having been withdrawn as unsound.

#### ⚠ AND THIS SECTION WAS CLAIMED BEFORE IT EXISTED

The commit immediately before this one — `docs: §3.2's eighteenth delta, §4a's Task 6 section,
the handover` — says in its subject and its body that `§4a` has a Task 6 section. **It did
not.** The script that writes this section needs the final figures as arguments, the figures
were still being measured, and the commit went in anyway.

That is **QA H-1's defect, repeated by me inside the commit that was fixing it** — the same
"claimed before written" pattern `§0`'s debt cell records for `R-003`, `R-004`, `R-006` and
`R-035`, and the reason this task's reviews raised it to a High. It is recorded here rather
than hidden by an amend, because the useful artefact is not a clean history, it is the count
of how many times this one keeps happening: **three times in this branch** — the `§5` rows,
this section, and the `§3.2` delta number I wrote as "seventeenth" without looking.

The narrow lesson, which is narrower than "check your claims": **a commit message that
describes a file's contents is itself a claim about measured state, and this project has no
mechanical control over commit messages at all.** `git` will not tell you that a subject
line is false. The only two controls that exist here are the `commit-msg` conventional-commit
hook, which checks shape and not truth, and a reader. Every other claim in this repository
has a test, a proof script or a grep behind it; this class has nothing, which is why it is the
one that recurs.

#### The branch name, and why the RECORD moved rather than the branch (2026-10-28)

`QRPAGER-13 §6`'s *Definition of Done* said branch **`task-6-tenant-provisioning`**. The branch
that exists, carries ten commits and carries the annotated `task-6` tag is
**`task-6-provisioning`**, and every record in this repository now names that one — `§0`, this
section, and `QRPAGER-13 §0` SR-5, with the Jira ticket's `§6` corrected to match.

**Why it was cut under that name.** The rank-1 prompt's second line reads, verbatim: *"Branch
task-6-provisioning off task-5-auth-rbac at the task-5 tag (5a227f8)."* The ticket said the
other. `§0` makes the chat message rank 1 and the ticket rank 3, so the prompt's spelling won
and the divergence was recorded as SR-5 rather than resolved silently. **Muhammad's reading is
that the ticket's name was the correction and should have won.** The prompt's text is quoted
here so the disagreement rests on a fact rather than on either side's memory; it changes
nothing about what to do now, because both readings end at the same place — the repository has
one branch and the records must name it.

**Why the branch is NOT renamed.** It carries a **pushed annotated tag**. `§10` makes the tag
the delivery record, so a rename would leave `task-6` pointing into a ref name that no longer
exists on the remote, and would require deleting and recreating the tag — the operation Task 2
had to perform once already (recorded above: the remote tag was deleted and recreated on
`2e42267` rather than force-moved, precisely so it got its own CI run in its own concurrency
group). Renaming to tidy a name would spend a verdict to buy nothing.

**The rule this settles, which is the part worth keeping:** when a record and the repository
disagree about a *name*, the repository wins and the record moves — because the repository is
the thing a later reader will `git checkout`, and `§8` stops for a record that disagrees with
it. That is the opposite direction from a record and the repository disagreeing about a
*measurement*, where `§4a` has corrected the record every time precisely because the
measurement is the fact. Names are facts about the repo; figures are facts about the code.

### 5.1 Ledger sweep of 2026-10-27 — every row read against its own owner

Run at the start of Task 5, before any Task 5 work, because `§5` had grown to ninety-odd rows
and **every `§11` reviewer reads the table**. The sweep's question was narrow and mechanical:
**is any row owned by a task that is already tagged, and still open?** A row owned by finished
work is either done or mis-owned, and neither of those is "open".

**Counts. Before: 99 rows — 26 closed, 73 open. After the sweep: 99 rows — 30 closed, 69 open.**
**And at the end of Task 5: 103 rows — 34 closed, 69 open**, after the task closed the four rows
it owned (`R-006`, `R-007`, `R-035`, `R-081`) and wrote four (`R-100` … `R-103`). Four of the open
69 are *part*-closed: `R-045`, `R-059`, `R-088`, `R-091`.
No row was created by the sweep; `§11`'s *corrected in place, never as a new risk row* applies
to everything it found.

**⚠ THESE FOUR NUMBERS ARE A CORRECTION. The first draft of this section published "31 → 35
closed, 68 → 64 open" and all four were wrong**, re-measured on 2026-10-28 before any Task 5
implementation commit. The sweep's *effect* is unchanged — it closed exactly four rows — but
the figures around it were taken with a grep and the grep was counting things that are not
closures. Recorded as a correction rather than silently replaced, because `R-025` is the
standing row about exactly this and the defect landing in the sweep's own arithmetic is worth
more than a tidy number.

**The counting rule, stated so the next count is reproducible: a row is CLOSED when nothing
remains for any owner, and OPEN when any part remains, however much of it is done.** By that
rule the table is **30 closed · 69 open**, and **five of the 69 are *part*-closed**: `R-007`
(Task 2's half closed at `2655bdd`, Task 5 still owns the role matrix and the lower-casing),
`R-045` (the "no test covers it" half closed at Task 3, the row stays open for Task 12),
`R-059` (the local half closed at Task 3 ahead of its owner, CI's half still Task 12's),
`R-091` (the `ORDER BY` half done, the figure and the product question still open) and `R-088`
(three of four coverage gaps, see its row).

**Why a grep disagrees, in both directions.** Searching the table for `CLOSED` returns **36**.
Two of those are not closures at all: `R-088`'s new Review-by cell reads **PART-CLOSED**, and
**`R-047` contains the phrase "`/readyz` fails CLOSED with no snapshot"** — a fail-open/fail-closed
posture, not a closure record. `R-047` is **open**, owned by Task 13, and its Review-by is unmet.
The other four of the 36 are the part-closed rows above, which declare a closure and stay open.

**Tags that exist, which is what "already tagged" was measured against:** `task-0`, `task-1`,
`task-2`, `task-3` (`f30bd24`), `task-4` (`55a4f98`). Tasks 3 and 4 are tagged and **not**
merged, by instruction.

## 6. Open items

- Billing / subscriptions: not in the Blueprint and not requested by the client. **Out of scope until stated.**
- Launch tier: unset by design until Task 14.
- **Queue transport for push dispatch.** The Blueprint specified SQS. The design is an outbox table plus a worker, which satisfies the guarantee — "ready" commits instantly, the send happens behind it with retries — independently of transport. Laravel's Redis queue is the default. **Task 13 decides whether the launch tier needs SQS instead, and Task 14 measures it.** Do not assume either.
- **Data migrations under FORCE RLS — settled, and corrected.** The pattern is `PLAN.md §2.10`. It was wrong until 2026-10-25 (H-1, QA review of task-1): it opened by enumerating tenants with a plain owner read, which returns **zero rows** under FORCE RLS, so the loop body never ran and a backfill would have silently done nothing. The list now comes through one audited `withoutTenantScope()` read; the per-tenant work still needs no bypass. `DataMigrationPatternTest` proves both halves, including at transaction level 1, which is where every migration body runs.
- **`outbox` and `audit_log` retention is unassigned.** Both grow without bound (§2.11): no grant deletes a `sent` or `dead` outbox row, and `audit_log` is append-only, so pruning it can only ever be a partition drop, never a `DELETE`. Nothing breaks before launch; it is a disk bill that grows. **Decide in Task 13 (storage sizing) and measure in Task 14.** Do not let the first person who notices invent a `DELETE`, because the trigger will refuse it.
- **Platform-admin cross-tenant reads are not on the §4 named list.** Task 6 builds a platform dashboard, a restaurants list and an audit-log viewer, all of which read across tenants. `§4 › Tenancy` names exactly four cross-tenant paths and says "adding one requires editing this file first". Task 1 deliberately built **no** policy for these: `qrpager_app` has no cross-tenant policy anywhere. Task 6 must either get §4 amended (a rank-2 edit, so the user's call) or go through §2.8's `SECURITY DEFINER` recipe with its own authorisation. **Raised now so Task 6 does not discover it mid-wizard.**
- **Platform-scope `audit_log` rows (`tenant_id` NULL) can currently be written only through the owner bypass.** `app` holds `INSERT` but the isolation policy's `WITH CHECK` compares `tenant_id` to the context, and `NULL = x` is never true. Task 6's "platform admin actions all land in `audit_log`" therefore needs a decision: an `INSERT`-only policy allowing `tenant_id IS NULL` (write-only for the app, readable only through §2.8), or every platform action naming a tenant. Not invented here.
- **Laravel wraps the driver error — settled at Task 2 (`2655bdd`, wired in at `ccca185`).** `QueryException::getCode()` is not reliably the SQLSTATE, and the shape of the unreliability is now measured rather than warned about: for STATEMENT errors `getCode()` and `getPrevious()->errorInfo[0]` **agree** — `42P01`, `22P02`, `22012` — which is exactly why a `getCode()`-based reader looks correct. For a CONNECTION-level failure they do not: a refused connection and a wrong password both give `getCode()` = the integer **`7`** where the SQLSTATE is **`08006`**. So anything built on `getCode()` printed "SQLSTATE 7" for precisely the failures an operator most needs named — and `08006` is also how a saturated role `CONNECTION LIMIT` arrives at the client, never `53300`. `App\Platform\Database\DriverError` is the single reader: `sqlState()` walks the chain for a `PDOException` with an `errorInfo`, and `sqlStateForMessage()` returns a real SQLSTATE or an empty string rather than a wrong code. `tests/TestCase.php::sqlState()` keeps the same shape for the suite.

### API versioning — the policy for a breaking change

Written here at Task 2, which the `§3` gate requires ("the versioning policy for a breaking change is
written into §6") and `D6` places in this file rather than in `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §6`: it is a
project decision, not a universal rule, so it belongs at rank 3.

**The surface.** Every public API route is under `/v1`, served by `bootstrap/app.php`'s
`apiPrefix: 'v1'`. Enforced by `tests/Feature/Http/RouteSurfaceTest.php`, which fails on any public
route outside `/v1` that is not in a written allowlist.

**The two exceptions, and why they are not versioned.** `/healthz` and `/readyz`. A load balancer's
health-check path is infrastructure configuration, and versioning it means the target group has to be
reconfigured because the API's major version changed — a deploy-time coupling with no benefit. They are
on their own middleware group, carrying no rate limiter, no tenant middleware and no load shedding,
which is the mechanism behind `§4 › Edge & ops`'s "while health and readiness keep answering". Approved
by the user on 2026-10-26, after confirming that nothing called the route being replaced: Laravel's
`/up` was referenced in exactly one place outside `vendor/` — `bootstrap/app.php` — and by no
healthcheck, no CI step, no test and no document.

**A published path is never changed in place.** Once a path under `/v1` has been deployed, its
behaviour may only be extended compatibly. The following are **breaking** and may not be done to a
published path:

| Breaking | Compatible |
| --- | --- |
| removing or renaming a field in a response | adding a field |
| narrowing an accepted input, or making an optional field required | widening an accepted input, or adding an optional field |
| changing a field's type, or the meaning of a value | adding a value to an enum **only** where the client is specified to ignore unknown values |
| changing a status code for an existing outcome | adding a status code for a new outcome |
| removing a route, or changing what a path matches | adding a route |

**How a breaking change ships.** A new prefix — `/v2` — carrying only the routes that change. `/v1`
keeps working until it is retired. The two live side by side; there is no "upgrade in place" path, and
no version negotiation by header: the version is in the path, where a CDN, a log line and a WAF rule
can all see it. Retiring `/v1` is its own decision with its own notice period, taken when a tenant is
actually on `/v2`.

**The enum caveat is not theoretical.** `pager_status` is a shared contract generated into
`packages/contracts` at Task 8 (ADR-003) from the PHP enum. Adding a case is a **breaking** change to
any client that switches exhaustively on it, which a TypeScript client does by default. So a new
`pager_status` value is a `/v2` change unless the client contract states that unknown values map to a
documented fallback — a decision for the task that adds the case, recorded with it.

**What enforces this.** The committed OpenAPI document. CI regenerates it from the routes and fails on
a diff, so a breaking change cannot reach `main` without appearing in a reviewed spec diff. The
document is the record of what was published; this policy is what may be done to it.

### Deliberately different from the Blueprint — recorded so nobody "fixes" it

| The Blueprint said                                         | We do not                              | Why                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Split the notification service from the API                | One Laravel application                | That split existed to stop SSE connection load from taking down order handling. **O2 removed SSE.** Web Push needs no open connection, so the load it protected against does not exist. Revisit only if Task 14 measures API contention. |
| Alarms and dashboards in CloudWatch, X-Ray **and Grafana** | CloudWatch + X-Ray only                | Three observability surfaces for one product is three places to look during an incident. Add Grafana only if a named need appears.                                                                                                       |
| Redis in cluster mode, with a channel per instance         | Single ElastiCache, no pub/sub fan-out | That design existed to fan SSE events out to every instance holding connections. **O2 removed it.** Cluster mode for the status projection is a **Task 13 sizing decision measured in Task 14**, not an architectural one.               |
